newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Hunger drove N.Koreans on 10-month trip to South.
newsitem.headline: Hunger drove N.Koreans on 10-month trip to South.

text.p: Worsening hunger drove eight North Korean defectors to embark on a 10-month odyssey across China and the sea to finally reach South Korea, local media reports said on Thursday.

The Chosun Ilbo newspaper quoted members of the two families, who arrived on Wednesday, as saying they decided to flee the Stalinist state after seeing seven people in a town of 90 families starve to death between January and March last year.

A spokesman for Seoul's Agency for National Security Planning declined to give details about the latest in a series of escapes from the North, which is on the brink of famine following several years of chronic food shortages.
"They are being investigated and we have nothing to make public yet," the spokesman said by telephone.

Local media reports also said Kim Young-jin, who claimed to be a relative by marriage to the wife of the late North Korean leader Kim Il-sung, feared being punished for having listened to a radio broadcast from the South.
Kim Il-sung died in 1994 and his son Kim Jong-il now leads the nation, although he has yet to assume the key posts of state president and general-secretary of the ruling Workers Party.

The agency said the North Korean defectors, including five children aged from 10 to 16, had sought asylum after entering Southern waters following a boat trip in freezing weather across the Yellow Sea between China and the Korean peninsula.

They left Mundok near Pyongyang last March and arrived in Musan near the northeastern border with China before crossing the Tumen River to go on a journey that included Chinese cities such as Yanji, Beijing and Dalian, the Chosun Ilbo said.
The Chosun Ilbo, a leading national daily, and several other newspapers published excerpts of a diary written by Kim Hae-kwang, 14, the second son of Kim Young-jin.
The diary said: "My class has 42 students but only half of them are attending. It's because of hunger."
He also said in the diary: "The train bound for Musan turned into a shambles with people looking for their baggage, children crying from hunger and women yelling hysterically."
An increasing number of North Koreans have fled the hermit nation and sought asylum in the South following several years of chronic food shortages.
The two Koreas remain technically at war after the 1950-53 Korean conflict ended in a truce and not a peace agreement.
In its latest report, the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) said the food shortage would worsen this year and require major international help to ensure minimum needs were met.
The South Korean Red Cross said on Monday it would resume food shipments to the North this month for the first time since a North Korean submarine incursion froze food aid.
It said 15,000 pairs of socks donated by groups in South Korea and 300 tonnes of flour would be sent around January 25.

All contacts with the North were halted after a submarine dropped 26 armed intruders on a Southern beach in September. Pyongyang issued a rare apology last month that satisfied Seoul, which returned the remains of 24 of the infiltrators who were shot and killed.
Last month, a family of 16 and a security guard, the largest group of North Korean defectors since the 1950-53 war, arrived in Seoul six weeks after traveling down the length of China to Hong Kong.
The recent rise in defections has been a propaganda coup for South Korea but has also sparked fears about how Seoul would cope if the trickle became a tide of refugees.
